what_it_does: When a chip design is printed onto a silicon wafer, the lithography process (using light to etch patterns) distorts the intended shapes, so engineers pre-distort the 'mask' — the stencil used to expose the wafer — to compensate. This correction step is called mask optimization (MO), and it must be done across an entire chip layout, which is enormous. Existing AI approaches work only on small clips of the layout at a time and do not capture how patterns in one region affect distant regions, leading to limited corrections and poor generalization across different designs. This paper proposes treating the full-chip mask correction as a visual understanding task and applying a large foundation model (similar in spirit to the large vision models used for image recognition) to the whole layout at once. The model includes a specially designed feature extractor that understands how polygons in different parts of the layout interact with each other over long distances, and it explicitly encodes the physics of light optics and the chemistry of the photoresist used in manufacturing. Because the approach learns from diverse mask patterns across many designs, it is expected to generalize better than clip-by-clip methods.
